item.title: If You’re Over 40, You’re Ready to Use A.I.
item.description:
There is a stern warning to anyone who wants to study kabbalah, a mystical tradition within Judaism that seeks to uncover the hidden nature of God and the universe: Just wait. In traditional practices, prospective students are urged to delay their studies until they reach the age of 40, at which point it is assumed they will have developed the inner ballast to withstand what they might encounter.

We should consider doing something similar for artificial intelligence.

I understand how extreme this may sound, especially now that artificial intelligence has already entered seemingly every area of our lives. But the extremity is the point.

We have been so quick to treat access to new technology as an inevitability that we have failed to question whether every powerful tool should be placed in the hands of every developing mind the moment it becomes available.

I also see this as more than a theoretical issue. In the graduate program where I teach brand strategy, my students recently completed thesis projects that involve repositioning brands or concepts that have fallen out of pace with culture. At the beginning of the school year, we asked them to sign a document acknowledging that they understood the rules governing their use of artificial intelligence: They were allowed to use A.I. for research and for the visualization of ideas, but they were instructed not to use it to replace original thinking and writing.

We reminded them of these rules again at the beginning of the thesis process, because the thesis is not simply a deliverable or an exercise in presentation, but the place where their thinking is supposed to become visible. Because brand strategy is so dependent on the compelling communication of ideas, this is the part of the program in which students have to wrestle with language, evidence, doubt and the responsibility of making an argument they can confidently stand behind and defend.

Despite the agreement they signed and several serious reminders, we suspected that some students had indeed used A.I. in place of their own original writing. When we asked, they squirmed and then admitted they had used A.I. to augment and synthesize their writing. I found their use of the word “augment” especially revealing because it allowed the act to appear smaller than it was; it made the intervention of A.I. in their work sound cosmetic and clerical, when what was actually being altered was the student’s relationship to struggle, authorship and accountability.

I don’t think my students are inherently deceitful or that they set out to behave with contempt for the work, the program or their faculty. While I was grateful that they readily admitted to the infraction, I wonder if they understood the gravity of the situation. This is what scares me most, as it is something far more ordinary: Students seem unable to resist the ease that L.L.M.s provide them to wrestle with and craft the construction of their ideas, and are incapable of tolerating the discomfort of searching for language when language can be produced for them. They also seem unwilling to stay inside difficulty long enough for the difficulty to teach them something they will likely never learn any other way.

There is something druglike about using A.I., not because it necessarily produces pleasure, but because it removes a particular kind of pain. A person who grows up with A.I. may never know the necessary agony of a blank page, the false start, the dull vocabulary and the private embarrassment of a first draft. A student who relies on A.I. too early will likely never sit long enough with confusion to distinguish it from failure.

Confusion is a necessary state wherein they learn how to think for themselves. (Interesting turn of phrase, isn’t it? As though a person could think for anyone else.) Language is not merely how we express ourselves; it is one of the ways we become ourselves. We write in order to find out what we think, we revise in order to discover whether or not we believe it, and we speak, stumble, clarify, retract and try again and again in order to understand the space between ideas and truth.

The Jewish tradition treats kabbalah as knowledge that requires readiness. Actual wisdom doesn’t come instantly, and it certainly doesn’t arrive fully fluent. Wisdom is the slow education of the self, built by lived experience. Often we resist it, and more often, it requires us to revise what we once thought we knew. This can be humiliating, but that is why wisdom is also associated with growth. There is a reason we were told “No pain, no gain” and “I learned this the hard way” over and over as children.

I will admit, for a mature person, A.I. can be useful. A formed mind can argue or wrangle with the machine, reject its false polish and recognize when the language it constructs to redescribe the world has become too smooth or soulless. Someone who has lived with words long enough can sense when a sentence has not been earned, and someone who has already developed a voice can use the machine without allowing the machine to become the voice.

An unformed person may not know the difference, and that is also where danger lies. The obvious problem is cheating. But cheating is only the most visible and least interesting part of the problem. The more profound risk is that young people will use artificial intelligence to bypass the development of their own interior lives and fail to hone their actual intelligence.

We do not wait for children to turn 16 to hand them car keys because cars are evil, and we do not insist that surgeons train for years because scalpels are immoral. We build thresholds around powerful things because power requires judgment, and judgment can’t be downloaded or installed. Before a person asks a machine to write for them, they should know what it feels like to write from the depths of their own uncertainty and identity. Before a person lets a machine imitate their voice, they should have endured the long, uneven, often humiliating process of acquiring one.

Of course, a rule like this is impossible as policy, and surely 40 is very late to adopt A.I. I know that artificial intelligence will not be held back by a cultural admonition, a syllabus clause, a signed agreement or even a teacher’s plea. There will be no collective vow of restraint, because the technology is already woven into the systems in which we are learning and working.

But impossibility does not make the argument meaningless. Sometimes a rule is valuable not because it can be enforced, but because it tells us what a culture reveres. The old caution around kabbalah suggests that some knowledge is not improved by premature access. Kabbalah reveals that depth requires preparation, that mystery should not be consumed as content and that the human approaching any text matters as much as the text itself.

We need a similar caution now, not because artificial intelligence is mystical or sacred, but because it enters us through language, and language is the medium through which we know ourselves.

The risk of relying on artificial intelligence is not just that it may hallucinate or outright lie, because people lie, too. The fact that artificial intelligence is often biased, derivative and bland? Frankly, human beings are capable of all of that, as well. The more prescient danger is that artificial intelligence provides the appearance of comprehension without the burden of experience, and because its language arrives instantly and obediently, it can feel less like a tool and more like wisdom.

Debbie Millman is a designer and brand strategist, the host of the podcast “Design Matters” and the chair of the Master’s in Branding program at the School of Visual Arts.

item.title: New York Museum Misused $597,000 in Federal Funds, Investigators Say
item.description:
Federal investigators said high-ranking administrators at the New York State Museum in Albany directed a subordinate to falsify time sheets, allowing the state to improperly draw down $597,624 in federal grants from 2020 to 2022.

The findings were published in a summary of an investigation conducted by the U.S. Department of Interior’s Office of Inspector General, after reporting by The New York Times about the fraud allegations.

The Times reported in late 2024 that a former payroll employee at the museum, Brian Slater, had accused a manager of directing him to submit false time sheets as part of a ploy to bilk federal funds from the U.S. Geological Survey and that high-ranking state officials had “supported” the fraud.

The investigation, which the inspector general’s office did in conjunction with the New York State comptroller, Thomas P. DiNapoli, focused on whether state grant administrators had compelled a museum employee to “fraudulently overreport” his work on a Geological Survey mapping project in order to qualify for federal grants.

“We substantiated the allegations,” the summary report says. The investigation determined that state museum administrators “instructed their employees to submit inaccurate time sheets reflecting inflated levels of involvement” in the program and improperly reallocated funds to pay staff salaries.

Investigators delivered the report to the director of the U.S. Geological Survey, which falls under the Interior Department, so he could pursue “the potential collection of lost revenues and any other action deemed appropriate,” the report said.

The report comes almost three years after the New York State Education Department, which oversees the museum, quickly closed its own investigation after declaring it unsubstantiated, records obtained by The Times show.

“It is not possible to conclude that there is mismanagement or fraud,” the internal state report said.

The state Education Department has acknowledged the overall findings by the Office of Inspector General. An Education department spokesman, JP O’Hare, said the agency was “fully transparent and cooperative throughout this process,” adding that officials were “prepared to reimburse any grant funding ultimately determined not to have been supported by the required state match.”

Mr. Slater said in a statement to The Times that he suspected that state officials would be more willing to repay what was owed to Washington rather than directly punish those implicated in the fraud.

“While repaying funds may address the financial impact on U.S.G.S., it does not address the harm done to museum employees who were pressured into participation for fear of job loss,” Mr. Slater said. “More importantly, allowing individuals implicated in proven wrongdoing to face no meaningful consequences will only further undermine staff morale and institutional credibility.”

Matt Sweeney, a spokesman for the state comptroller, referred questions about any recoupment of revenue to federal authorities, but said their joint investigation “found that the museum had illegitimately billed the grant for nearly $600,000 in hours spent by employees on other projects.”

John T. McDonald III, a state assemblyman whose district includes parts of Albany County, said the Education Department must identify any gaps in oversight to “prevent this from happening again.”

Mr. McDonald said the report was a reminder of how far the museum fell into disrepair and bureaucratic mismanagement — a chapter he thinks the state is finally moving past thanks to Gov. Kathy Hochul’s plans to renovate parts of downtown Albany.

Ms. Hochul and education officials are embarking on a $150 million renovation of the museum as part of that renovation, and Mr. McDonald said he was encouraged by what he has heard from both leaders and rank-and-file employees, even as he worries that internal accountability measures need to be strengthened.

“We’re on the dawn of a new era with the museum,” he said. “What you’re bringing to light is really — I’d like to think — a remnant of the past.”

item.title: Investigation of School Epstein Helped Finds Abuses Went Beyond Him
item.description:
Dozens of former students of the Interlochen Center for the Arts in Michigan, where Jeffrey Epstein is said to have encountered some of his earliest victims, told a law firm hired by the school that they had been sexually abused by teachers, staff members, trustees and others affiliated with the institution in episodes ranging from the 1950s to the 2010s.

In a report released on Tuesday, after almost two years of interviews, the law firm presented firsthand accounts of Interlochen alumni, who said they had been subjected to misconduct ranging from grooming and flirting to intercourse. The report said that some 70 of the former students described physical abuse and identified the perpetrators as 47 adults affiliated with the center.

The report, which is 97 pages long, said that some of the adults figured in multiple accounts that stretched over decades, but that a majority of the episodes had occurred several decades ago and claims of abuse had dropped sharply since 2000.

“Many alums detailed the impact that this conduct had on them,” said the report, from the Sanghavi Law Office, a Massachusetts-based firm. “Some shared that the impacts were significant and lasted well after they graduated from, or otherwise left, Interlochen.”

The arts institution, which was founded in the 1920s, is both a year-round boarding school for teenage prodigies and a summer camp. It is known for its rigorous instruction and recreational diversions in a pastoral campus set near two lakes, and has long drawn a selective group of young musicians and other aspiring artists, including Mr. Epstein, who attended as a teenage bassoonist.

In recent years, Interlochen also became known as the place where Mr. Epstein, a celebrated donor to the school, returned to mingle with students, several of whom later said they had been subjected to his grooming and abuse.

Though parents of two girls who attended Interlochen have said that decades ago they told the school that their daughters were discomforted by Mr. Epstein’s attention, Interlochen officials have said the records they have on hand do not contain any indication of complaints about Mr. Epstein before his 2008 conviction in Florida of a sex offense involving a minor. The school has said it then cut all ties to him.

In a statement released alongside the report, Interlochen officials expressed their regrets.

“On behalf of Interlochen, we are deeply sorry for the harm experienced by members of our community and extend our apologies to those impacted by abuse at Interlochen,” Trey Devey, the school’s president, and Barrett Rollins, the chair of its board, said in a public letter to the Interlochen community.

“We have provided the names of all individuals accused of misconduct to the Grand Traverse County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office and the Grand Traverse County Sheriff’s Office, which will determine if there is a viable pathway to prosecution or other steps that could be taken to promote accountability or minimize current risk to students at other institutions,” the letter added.

Mr. Epstein was 14 when he attended the camp on a scholarship in 1967. Between 1990 and 2003, he returned as a donor, directing more than $400,000 to Interlochen, including $200,000 to build the Jeffrey E. Epstein Scholarship Lodge, created to house visitors and parents.

Records released by the Department of Justice and the school indicate that Mr. Epstein stayed in the lodge on some of his visits to Interlochen in the 1990s and in 2000. It was during those visits that Mr. Epstein is known to have met some of the earliest victims of his grooming and abuse.

The report included the accounts of two of the three former Interlochen students who have described disturbing encounters with Mr. Epstein. In one case, a woman told the investigators of going to meet him at the campus lodge where “Epstein engaged in sexual conduct with her, brushing against her body over her clothes, in a manner in which he indicated was accidental,” the report said.

The woman also told investigators that Mr. Epstein paid for her to visit him in New York on three occasions when she was a student.

“She described being in a room with Epstein in New York, and that his hands were on her,” the report said. It noted that “this alum said that on occasions when she and Epstein were crossing the road, he put his hand on her crotch.”

The report included additional claims by a third former Interlochen student who told investigators that Mr. Epstein had paid for her to fly to New York the summer after she graduated, and that she had given him a massage at his home and he “may have asked her to remove her top.” Her mother called Interlochen, her mother told investigators, to warn the school that Mr. Epstein was “preying on their students,” but they said no one from Interlochen had followed up.

In 2009, Interlochen renamed the Epstein lodge and removed a plaque that acknowledged his philanthropy. Mr. Epstein died in 2019. In June, Interlochen demolished the lodge as it continued to work to shed any connection to its former benefactor.

The episodes related in the investigators’ report occurred on and off campus, including in faculty houses.

While the report did not make any formal findings about Interlochen’s security protocols, it highlighted gaps that had, for example, allowed faculty and staff members to be alone with students while giving donors or trustees open access to the campus. None of the 47 adults referred to in the report are currently employed or affiliated with Interlochen, the school said.

The report noted instances in which the school took action at the time to fire employees when accusers came forward. It also listed new protocols Interlochen had put in place in recent years, such as enhanced reporting practices, improved background checks and 24/7 supervision of the campus. Some 240 cameras have been installed around its 1,200 acres.

In the wake of the report’s findings, Interlochen said it was making counseling support available for former students affected by the abuse. It also said it would remove naming credits on, for example, buildings if doing so was found to be warranted. The school said it had already changed the name of a building named after a former trustee who was associated with the school from 1970 to 1999.

“Interlochen today is fundamentally different from the institution described in this report,” the Interlochen officials wrote in the public letter.

The school said the investigators spoke with about 120 former students for the review.

Mr. Devey, who has been Interlochen’s president since 2017, credited a former student, who came forward in 2024 with a complaint from the 1970s, with spurring the broader investigation.

“It’s clearly been a difficult process for our community,” he said, “but I think an essential one.”
